messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 80
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Data Scientist
- Trauma Type: Relief worker in war zone
- Pcl5: 50

# The Weight of What He Carried Home

Boon-Nam is an eighty-year-old Vietnamese-born man who, even now, spends his mornings hunched over a laptop, running statistical models for a small nonprofit that tracks global humanitarian crises. His colleagues, most of them young enough to be his grandchildren, know him as precise, methodical, and quietly brilliant. What they do not know is that the data he analyzes — displacement figures, casualty estimates, population movements — sometimes makes it impossible for him to eat lunch.

In 1972, when Boon-Nam was in his late twenties, he volunteered with an international relief organization operating near the Cambodian border during the heaviest years of the conflict. He had trained as a statistician and believed, with the earnestness of a young man who had read too many hopeful books, that good data could save lives. What he found instead was that the numbers never moved fast enough to outpace the dying. For fourteen months he worked in makeshift field hospitals and transit camps, cataloguing the dead and the displaced, negotiating supply routes, and watching children arrive at the camps in conditions he still cannot fully describe, even to himself. One afternoon — he remembers it was a Tuesday because he had just completed a weekly report — a mortar strike hit a shelter he had helped construct two weeks earlier. He was fifty meters away. He ran toward it. He has never entirely forgiven himself for what he found, and for the fact that he survived it.

He came home, married a woman named Linh, built a career in data science, and raised two daughters. For decades he managed by staying busy. Linh understood, without him ever saying so directly, that certain topics were closed. She would change the television channel when war footage appeared. She kept the house quiet in the mornings. When she died four years ago, the structure she had quietly maintained around him collapsed.

Now Boon-Nam lives alone in a tidy apartment in Melbourne. Sleep has become his adversary. He wakes most nights between two and three in the morning with his heart hammering, the smell of smoke and something metallic so vivid he checks the hallway for fire. He rarely remembers a specific dream, only the sensation of being back there, of the ground being wrong beneath his feet. During the day he is functional, even sharp, but he moves through the world with a vigilance that exhausts him — sitting with his back to walls in cafes, scanning exits, startling badly when a door slams in the office.

He has largely stopped socializing. His daughters call regularly, and he is warm with them, but he deflects their concern with gentle humor and changes the subject. He has not told them what he saw in 1972. He does not believe it would be fair to put it into their minds.

What troubles him most, he says, is not the nightmares but the numbness that has settled over his days since Linh died. He used to feel pride in his work. Now he looks at a dataset representing ten thousand displaced persons and feels something that is not quite sadness and not quite nothing — a hollow recognition, as though he already knew how this story ends. He wonders sometimes whether he has simply processed too much suffering over too many decades for ordinary feeling to reach him anymore.

He came to therapy at his younger daughter's gentle insistence. He sat in the first session with his hands folded in his lap and his posture very straight, and said, with careful politeness, that he was not sure he believed talking would change anything that had already happened. Then he paused, looked at the window, and said that he had not spoken about Cambodia to another person since Linh's funeral, when he had stood at her grave and whispered an apology he still cannot fully explain.
